steps.action:
# The Last Light

The fog came in like something living.

Maren had watched it roll across the water for thirty years, and she still couldn't decide if it moved with intention or merely with the indifference of weather. Tonight it swallowed the horizon whole, erasing the line between sea and sky until there was nothing beyond the lamp room glass but a soft, grey breathing.

She climbed the iron stairs the way she always did — seventy-two steps, her right hand trailing the curved wall, her boots finding each riser without her having to think about it. Her body knew this tower better than it knew anything else. Better than it had ever known another person.

The light was already turning. She checked the mechanism out of habit, running her fingers along the brass fittings, listening for the particular hum that told her everything was well. The great lens rotated in its bath of mercury, unhurried, throwing its beam out into the nothing at four-second intervals. Flash. Darkness. Flash. Darkness.

She had been twenty-six when she took the posting. The harbor master had looked at her application for a long time before he looked at her.

*It's lonely work,* he said.

*I know,* she said.

What she had meant was: I am already lonely. At least out there I'll have a reason.

---

The ships she had saved numbered somewhere in the dozens, though she had only witnessed one rescue directly. That had been in her third winter, a trawler called the *Saint Agatha* that had wandered into the shoals during a nor'easter that shook the tower like a fist. She had watched through binoculars as the crew launched a life raft into seas that seemed to have no interest in letting them survive. She had called the coast guard on the radio. She had kept the light burning though a transformer had blown and she'd had to switch to the backup generator by herself in the dark and the wind, using a flashlight held in her teeth.

All seven crew members survived.

She never met them. She read about the rescue in a newspaper someone left at the supply drop two weeks later. She clipped the article and put it in the binder she kept on the third shelf above her desk, between the tide tables and the maintenance logs.

There were eleven clippings in the binder now.

---

Her daughter called on Sundays, when the signal was good enough. Elena lived in the city and worked in finance and had her mother's grey eyes but her father's fundamental discomfort with silence. Their conversations had a quality of negotiation — Elena probing gently for some sign that Maren was ready to come in from the cold, Maren offering reassurances that she interpreted as the truth and Elena interpreted as stubbornness.

*Don't you want company, Mom?*

*I have company.*

*The seabirds don't count.*

*I wasn't going to say the seabirds.*

She was going to say the seabirds.

Also the harbor seals who pulled themselves onto the eastern rocks every morning like tired commuters. Also the container ships that passed at distance, lit up like small cities, heading for ports she had never visited. She knew their schedules. She tracked them in a logbook that no one had asked her to keep. When a familiar vessel appeared on time, right where she expected it, she felt something she could only describe as friendship, even though the crews had no idea she existed.

---

In October, the Coast Guard sent a letter.

The lighthouse was being automated. Modern GPS, improved chart accuracy, and a network of buoys had made the keeper position redundant. The process would take six months. She was welcome to stay on as a caretaker in a limited capacity, but the position would not be compensated at its current rate, and eventually, when the transition was complete, the residence would be repurposed.

She read the letter three times at the kitchen table while her coffee went cold.

Then she folded it carefully and put it in the binder, after the last clipping.

---

She didn't tell Elena right away. She wanted to live with it for a while, the way you live with a diagnosis before you start making calls. She wanted to understand what she actually felt before she was asked to explain it.

What she felt, she decided, was not grief exactly. It was something quieter. It was the feeling of being released from a post you had not realized you were still holding, by a war that had ended without announcement.

The light would keep turning. Ships would still find their way. That was the whole point. That had always been the whole point.

It was only that she had believed, without quite knowing it, that she was necessary. That somewhere in the arithmetic of the sea, her presence at the top of those seventy-two stairs mattered in a way that could not be replicated by a circuit board and a timer. And maybe it had. Maybe it had mattered enormously, in the years before the satellites, in the years before the buoys. Maybe the eleven clippings in her binder represented something real — lives preserved by the particular stubbornness of a woman who had confused her loneliness with a calling and found, against all reason, that the confusion had been correct.

Or maybe the harbor master had been right in a way she'd never let herself believe.

Maybe it had just been lonely work.

---

On the last night before the automated system went live, she climbed the stairs one final time on duty.

The fog was in again. The light turned. The beam swept out across the water and vanished and returned, patient and indifferent as the sea itself.

She stayed in the lamp room for four hours, though there was nothing she needed to do. She watched the light. She listened to the mechanism. Below her, the water moved in the dark, full of its usual dangers and its usual grace, doing what water does regardless of who is watching.

At some point near midnight, a container ship appeared at the edge of visibility — the *Wilhelmina K.*, familiar, right on schedule. Its lights moved steadily across the black water. It passed without incident.

She wrote it in the logbook.

Then she sat for a long time with her hands in her lap, listening to the hum of the great lens, and thought about how strange it was to love something that didn't need you back. How strange, and how completely ordinary. How almost everyone, she suspected, was doing exactly the same thing, in whatever tower they had climbed and refused to leave.

The light turned. The fog held. Somewhere out there, the sea went on.

She stayed until morning.
